Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette:
Koa, a 56-year-old detective from a small coastal town in Oceania, had spent decades of his life wrestling with a haunting past that had crept into his present. Memories of his childhood, particularly the physical abuse inflicted by his caregiver, had woven an intricate web of fear and distrust that seemed to shadow him at every turn. The trauma remained an unshakable presence, and as Koa prepared for yet another day on the job, the scent of burnt toast wafting through the precinct’s break room sent him spiraling. It was a trigger he had come to dread, a reminder of the chaos that had once filled his home. He had learned to associate that burnt smell with danger, a signal that something terrible was about to happen, just as it had in his youth. 

Koa's job as a detective often placed him in close proximity to victims, and he noticed how he instinctively flinched when he encountered individuals who resembled those he had failed to protect in the past. It was a reflex born not from malice but from a deep-seated trauma that convinced him he could never be safe around them. He had come to believe that if he could keep distance from people who looked even remotely like his childhood tormentors or their victims, he might stave off the memories that threatened to engulf him. He avoided certain clothing styles, opting for more neutral options that wouldn’t remind him of his past. 

As months turned into years, Koa’s coping strategies morphed into avoidance behaviors. He found himself withdrawing from social events, choosing solitary nights at home over gatherings with colleagues. The once vibrant detective had become a shadow of himself, his relationships strained. He often sat alone in his living room, staring blankly at the walls, the silence amplifying his hypervigilance. He was always on guard, convinced that the world was a perilous place where danger lurked around every corner. This constant state of alertness made it nearly impossible for him to fall asleep. The struggle to drift off became a nightly ritual of tossing and turning, his mind racing with images from the past that he desperately tried to detach from but could never fully escape.

When Koa attempted to explain his experiences to friends or even to himself, he often lost the thread of his thoughts, as if the trauma had rewired his brain to only present fragments of a larger, incomprehensible narrative. He felt an intense rage surging within him whenever the memories resurfaced. Each recall was like re-experiencing the physical pain, the helplessness. He frequently felt that he was a lousy coper, his reactions proving that he was somehow inadequate, a belief that was further solidified by his perception that the world was inherently unsafe. He attributed the abuse he endured to his own character, believing that he had somehow invited it upon himself.

The weight of his symptoms culminated in a particularly challenging week on the job. Koa had been called to investigate an assault case that bore a striking resemblance to the horrors of his childhood. As he stood at the crime scene, the smell of burnt rubber from a nearby dumpster triggered a flood of memories. He was overwhelmed, unable to focus on the task at hand. His physical reactions were intense; his heart raced, and his palms grew clammy. It was as if he had been thrust back to that dark time, and he could feel the rage building inside him, ready to spill over. 

After that incident, Koa realized he could no longer navigate his life by avoiding triggers. He felt trapped in a cycle of fear and isolation, desperately wanting to connect with his colleagues and engage in his work but feeling unable to do so. The burden of his past weighed heavily on him, and he recognized that it was time to seek help. As he sat in his car outside a therapist's office, he felt a mix of hope and fear. What frightened him most was the thought of revisiting those memories in detail, of facing the very pain he had spent a lifetime running from. He hoped, however, that through this journey, he might find a way to reclaim his life, to emerge from the shadows of his past and rebuild a future where he could finally feel safe.
